creative.body:
My husband has kissed me goodnight every night for twenty-two years. Same man. Same kiss. Never missed one.

Five months ago I started turning my head away. Every single night.

He never asked why. He just stopped trying.

He thinks it's him. It's not. And I can't tell him what it actually is.

Five months ago my doctor put me on Zepbound. I've lost twenty-two pounds. Dropped two pant sizes. My face is thinner. People I haven't seen in months are doing double takes. Everyone at my book club keeps telling me how good I look and I smile and say thank you with my mouth barely open because I've learned that wider than a half inch is a risk I can't calculate.

On paper I'm a success story. My doctor even said those words at my last appointment. "You're one of my success stories." I smiled with my lips pressed together and got out of there before anything came up.

She didn't ask about the burps. I didn't bring them up.

My name is Deborah. I'm 58. I taught fourth grade for twenty-six years before I retired. I live in a three-bedroom ranch house in a neighborhood where everybody waves when they drive past. I am not a dramatic person. I don't post on Facebook. I don't share things like this. But I need to tell you what Greg and I were like before, because you need to understand what I destroyed.

I need to tell you what Greg and I were like before, because you need to understand what I destroyed.

Twenty-two years married. He is not a complicated man. He reaches for me. That's what he does. That's what he's always done. Hand on my back while I'm standing at the stove. Arm around me on the couch during whatever we're watching. Goodnight kiss. Morning kiss. He'd come up behind me at the kitchen sink and rest his chin on my shoulder while I was doing dishes and I'd swat him away and laugh and he'd do it again the next night. He'd hold my hand in the car even though we're not twenty-five anymore. He'd pull me close in bed even when we were just sleeping.

It wasn't romantic in the movie sense. It was just how we worked. Two people who'd been together long enough that touching was like breathing. You don't think about it. You just do it. It's the background hum of a marriage that still likes itself.

I took all of it away from him. One flinch at a time.

The sulfur burps started around week six on Zepbound. I remember the first one. We were sitting at the kitchen table on a Sunday morning and I was telling Greg about something one of my book club friends had said and I felt it rising before I could stop it. Not a regular burp. This tasted like sulfur. Like rotten eggs had been heated up and shoved into the back of my throat. I clamped my mouth shut and turned my head toward the window and held my breath until it passed.

Greg said, "You okay?"

I said, "Wrong pipe."

That was the first lie. There would be hundreds more.

Over the next few weeks they got worse. Unpredictable. Violent almost. They'd come up mid-sentence. Mid-laugh. Mid-bite. Hot, rotten, and completely out of my control. One second I was fine. The next second my mouth filled with the taste of something dead and I'd press my lips together and pray nobody noticed.

I brought it up at my next doctor's appointment. Casually. Like it wasn't the thing I'd been thinking about every waking hour.

"I've been getting these burps," I said. "They taste like sulfur. They're pretty bad."

She nodded. Typed something. Said GI side effects are common on GLP-1 medications. Said they usually improve over time as the body adjusts. Said to try smaller meals, stay hydrated, maybe take a probiotic.

Then she moved on to how much weight I'd lost.

That was it. Thirty seconds on the thing that was dismantling my marriage and then we were celebrating how well the medication was working.

The first thing I changed at home was the mornings.

Greg and I have brushed our teeth at the same sink for twenty-two years. Side by side. He rinses, I spit, he makes a face, I elbow him. Stupid little marriage choreography that nobody plans and nobody notices until it's gone. After the burps started I began getting up fifteen minutes before him. Brushed my teeth alone. Rinsed with Listerine twice. Popped a mint before he even walked in. By the time he got to the bathroom I was already downstairs with my coffee, mouth sealed shut until I was sure nothing was coming up.

He never asked why I stopped waiting for him.

Then the car changed. Greg drives us everywhere. Has since our first date. I started cracking the window. Not all the way. Just an inch. In November, in January, in February when it was thirty-one degrees outside. He asked once if I was hot. I said I liked the fresh air. He turned the heat up for me and didn't mention it again.

I'd been holding my breath every time he leaned across the console to change the radio or touch my knee.

Then book club changed. First Wednesday of every month. Eight women. Wine, snacks, we pretend to talk about the book for twenty minutes and then gossip for two hours. I used to look forward to it. After the burps started I sat in the corner of Linda's sectional and held a throw pillow against my stomach like I was cold and every time I felt the pressure build I'd take a sip of wine to push it back down. Which made it worse. But at least the wine covered the taste.

One night Deborah was sitting next to me and I felt one come up and couldn't stop it. Not fully. I turned my head and breathed it toward the cushion and Deborah wrinkled her nose and looked around the room like she was trying to figure out where the smell was coming from.

She didn't say anything. Neither did I. I left twenty minutes early and told everyone I had a headache.

Then dinner changed. I stopped eating anything heavy after 3 PM because I'd figured out that eating was what triggered the worst burps. The more food sitting in my stomach, the worse it got by evening. So I'd eat a small lunch and then nothing. Which meant by the time Greg and I sat down for dinner together I'd move food around my plate and tell him I'd eaten late. A woman on a weight loss medication pretending she wasn't hungry. He believed me because why wouldn't he. I was losing weight. It made sense.

But the real reason I stopped eating dinner was because I knew what happened two hours later. The sulfur would build in my chest like a slow pressure and I'd have to either excuse myself to another room or press my lips together and breathe through my nose and hope it passed quietly. Most of the time it didn't pass quietly.

Then the couch changed.

We used to share a blanket. His end, my end, both of us gravitating toward the middle where the fabric bunched up between our legs. After the burps started I moved to the opposite end. If he shifted toward me I'd get up to refill my water or check my phone in the kitchen. He stopped shifting toward me.

Then the bedroom changed.

I started sleeping on my side, facing the wall. If I felt a burp coming in the middle of the night I could breathe it into the pillow instead of toward him. He'd reach his arm across the bed the way he'd always done and sometimes I'd feel his hand land on my hip and I'd hold completely still, mouth clamped, waiting for the pressure in my chest to pass before I could relax enough to let him touch me.

Some nights I couldn't relax. And his hand would just... retreat. Quietly. Like it had learned.

Then one night in December I woke up at 2 AM and rolled over and Greg was already facing the wall. Both of us. Facing opposite walls. In the bed we'd shared for twenty-two years, the bed where he used to pull me against his chest and fall asleep with his face in my hair. Both of us turned away from each other like strangers in a hotel.

He'd started adjusting too. I hadn't asked him to. He'd just learned. The way a dog learns not to come to you after you push it away enough times.

That thought is the one that made me cry in the bathroom at 2 AM.

I want to be very clear about something. None of this was a fight. None of this was a conversation. None of this was one of those marriage crises where someone yells and someone cries and you call your sister or your therapist. This was silent. This was me, night after night, week after week, training the man I love to stop touching me. And him being gentle enough to listen without ever making me say why.

By January he wasn't trying anymore.

No arm across the bed. No chin on my shoulder at the sink. No leaning in for a goodnight kiss. He'd say goodnight from his side and turn off the lamp and that was it. And I'd lie there in the dark facing the wall knowing that every single one of those lost touches was something I'd taken from him and he'd let me take it because that's the kind of man he is.

I tried everything I could think of to fix the burps.

Gas-X first. Three times a day for two weeks. Nothing. Not even a dent.

Then Pepto-Bismol before bed. The pink stuff. I kept a bottle in the bathroom cabinet behind the towels so Greg wouldn't see it and ask questions.

Then charcoal capsules someone on Facebook swore by. Ordered them at 11 PM after reading a thread where a woman said they "changed her life." They didn't change mine.

Then the probiotic. This one I remember because it cost more than my Zepbound copay. I drove to a health food store twenty minutes away because I didn't want to run into anyone I knew. The girl at the counter was maybe twenty-three. She said her mom had the same problem on Ozempic and this exact blend cleared it up in a week. I bought two bottles. Took them for three weeks. The only thing that changed was my bank account.

Every single product and not one of them made a difference. The sulfur kept coming. The mints kept multiplying. The distance kept growing.

I was starting to think this was just what Zepbound cost. Not the copay. Not the injection. The marriage. Five months of weight loss and the price was Greg's hand retreating in the dark.

One night in late January I almost told him. We were watching TV and he was on his end and I was on mine and I opened my mouth to say something. To explain. To tell him it wasn't him, it was never him, it was this thing happening inside me that I couldn't control. But I felt the pressure building in my chest and I closed my mouth and swallowed it and said "I'm going to bed" instead.

He said "Okay." Didn't look up.

That was the night I knew I'd broken something I might not be able to fix.

My friend Elaine turned 60 in February. Dinner at an Italian place downtown. Twelve of us around a long table with candles and bread baskets and wine and I almost didn't go. But Greg said I should. He said I hadn't gone out in weeks. He was right. I'd been avoiding any situation where food and people and conversation happened within breathing distance.

Patty was there. Elaine's college roommate. Retired OR nurse. We'd met a few times over the years. Patty is the kind of woman who spent thirty years in operating rooms and nothing embarrasses her. She talks about bodies the way mechanics talk about engines. She sat across from me.

I don't know why I told her. Maybe because she wasn't family. Maybe because I was on my second glass of wine and the shame had softened just enough to let the truth out. But somewhere between the appetizer and the main course I said it out loud for the first time to someone who wasn't a search engine.

That I was on Zepbound. That it was working for the weight. That sulfur burps were slowly destroying the physical part of my marriage. And that I didn't know how to make them stop.

She tilted her head. Looked at me the way nurses look at you when they're running through a differential in their head.

"When do the burps get worse?" she asked. "After you eat or before?"

I thought about it. "After. Always after. The more I eat, the worse they get."

She nodded slowly. "And when you wake up in the morning? Before you've eaten anything?"

"Almost never."

She picked up her wine glass. "That's interesting. That tells you where the problem is."

Then someone at the other end of the table asked about the tiramisu and the conversation moved on. Patty never circled back to it. She didn't need to. She'd planted something in my head that wouldn't let go.

That tells you where the problem is.

Where. Not what. Where.

That Thursday night I went down a rabbit hole.

Kitchen table. 11:47 PM. Greg was already asleep. I typed "why do GLP-1 medications cause sulfur burps" into Google.

The first few pages were the same useless advice I'd already tried. Drink more water. Take a probiotic. Try peppermint tea. Eat smaller meals. Avoid fatty foods. Everything I'd already been doing. Nothing that explained WHY.

But I kept going. Page four. Page five. Into the medical journals and the research abstracts and the forum threads buried so deep you'd never find them unless you were desperate at midnight with nothing left to lose.

And I found something I'd never seen anyone mention. Not my doctor. Not the Facebook groups. Not a single product I'd bought.

GLP-1 medications slow your stomach on purpose. That's the whole point. That's the mechanism. Your stomach empties slower, you feel full longer, you eat less, you lose weight. Every doctor knows this. Every patient knows this. It's on the box.

But here's what nobody connects to the sulfur.

When food sits in the stomach longer than it's supposed to, bacteria start breaking it down while it waits. Not in the intestine. In the STOMACH. And that bacterial breakdown produces hydrogen sulfide. Sulfur gas. The same compound that makes rotten eggs smell like rotten eggs. And that gas has nowhere to go but up. Through the esophagus. Out the mouth. Into whatever room you're standing in. Into whatever face is close enough to smell it.

That's the burps. That's the taste. That's what I'd been hiding from my husband for five months.

And Patty was right. The timing told me exactly where the problem was. After eating. Not before. Because the sulfur wasn't being made in my intestine. It was being made in my stomach, where the food was sitting and rotting because the medication was doing exactly what it was designed to do.

I kept reading. And it got worse.

The longer the stomach stays slow, the more food accumulates. The more food accumulates, the more bacteria feed. The more bacteria feed, the more sulfur gas builds. It doesn't level off. It doesn't get better on its own. It's a cycle that feeds itself for as long as the stomach isn't moving. Which is every single day you're on the medication.

That's when something clicked and I actually sat up straighter in my chair.

Every single product I'd been taking works BELOW the stomach. Downstream. In the intestine.

Gas-X breaks up gas bubbles in the intestine. My problem wasn't gas bubbles in the intestine. Pepto coats the lower GI tract. My problem wasn't in the lower GI tract. Probiotics colonize the gut. But the food wasn't even reaching the gut on schedule. It was decomposing in my stomach before it ever got there. Charcoal absorbs toxins in the digestive tract. But the sulfur was being manufactured in the stomach and rising UP, not moving down.

I'd been treating the wrong organ for five months.

Five months of mints and Listerine and Gas-X and Pepto and charcoal and a $52 probiotic and not one of them was even in the right zip code.

I kept going. Deeper into the research. What actually wakes a slow stomach back up? What neutralizes hydrogen sulfide where it's being produced? What supports the whole system downstream once the food finally starts moving through?

And I started finding answers. Real ones. In studies I'd never seen referenced anywhere.

Apigenin. A compound found in high concentrations in celery juice extract. Research showing it supports gastric motility. Helps wake the stomach up and get things moving again.

Chlorophyllin. Binds to sulfur compounds and neutralizes them. Not in the intestine. In the stomach. Where the gas is actually being made.

Prebiotic fiber. Feeds the beneficial bacteria downstream and supports healthy digestion once the food finally arrives where it's supposed to go.

Three things. Not one pill. Not one ingredient. Three specific functions working in three specific places at the same time.

I stayed up until almost 2 AM reading. Cross-referencing ingredients. Looking for anything that combined all three. Most products had one. Maybe two. None of them had all three together.

Then I found a small company in a forum thread. Someone had mentioned them in a comment with six upvotes buried thirty replies deep. The brand was called Motilli. Celery juice gummies.

I went to their site expecting to be disappointed. I'd already wasted money on five different products that did nothing.

And when I read the label I sat down at the kitchen table because every single thing I'd been researching was in there. Apigenin from celery juice extract for stomach motility. Chlorophyllin for neutralizing the sulfur gas. Prebiotic fiber for supporting everything downstream. All three. In one gummy.

I ordered one bottle. I didn't tell Greg.

First week, nothing changed. I almost texted Patty to tell her it was another dead end. Almost threw the bottle in the trash.

Second week. I was talking to my neighbor in the driveway after getting the mail and realized halfway through the conversation that I hadn't thought about my breath once. Not once. I'd been standing there with my mouth open, laughing, talking, for fifteen minutes without pressing my lips together or turning my head or calculating the wind direction. That hadn't happened in five months.

That night I ate dinner with Greg. Actual dinner. Chicken and rice and salad. I ate all of it. And I sat on the couch afterward and nothing happened. No pressure. No building. No excuse to leave the room.

By week three I woke up on a Saturday and rolled over to face Greg instead of the wall. He was already awake. He looked at me the way you look at someone when you're not sure if it's safe to reach. Like he was checking whether the rules had changed.

I took his hand under the covers.

That night he kissed me goodnight. Not the forehead. Not the careful peck from his side of the bed. He leaned in the way he used to lean in and I didn't turn my head.

He pulled back and looked at me and said, "You taste like you again."

I don't know why that was the sentence that broke me. But I cried. And he held me. And neither of us said anything about the last five months. We didn't have to.

His sister Denise started Mounjaro six weeks later. She called me the second week asking about sulfur burps. I told her about Motilli before they got bad enough to build a system around. She never had to carry mints in four different pockets. She never had to learn to sleep facing a wall. She never had to flinch.

If you know what sulfur tastes like at the back of your throat. If you've been turning away from the person you love because you can't control what comes out when you breathe. If you've built a system of mints and excuses and cracked windows to keep the distance manageable. If the person you share a bed with has quietly stopped reaching for you and you know exactly why. I need you to hear this.

The problem isn't your breath. It's not your intestine. It's your stomach. And the thing you need exists.

I left a link below. It's the same company I found at 2 AM at my kitchen table. If I'd found it three months earlier I never would have taught Greg to stop reaching for me.

Greg reaches for me again. Every single time, I reach back.
creative.title: I flinched away from my husband every night for four months and he never once asked why
